title: The (Un)importance of the Battle of Tours
gist: Daniel Wollenberg argues the Battle of Tours (732 CE) had negligible strategic significance and that its outsized reputation as the moment Charles Martel 'saved' Christian Europe from Islam is a myth manufactured by later Frankish propaganda and 18th-19th century historians. He traces how identitarian and far-right voices now weaponize that myth to frame Muslim immigration as a continuation of a 1,300-year civilizational war.

insights.claim: The consensus among contemporary historians such as Franco Cardini, Tomaz Mastnak, and James T. Palmer is that the Battle of Tours (732 CE) did not have a major impact on western European history and its significance was blown far out of proportion.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Establishes the scholarly baseline against which the political myth is measured, the article's central corrective.
insights.quote: Tours did not have a major impact on western European history and its significance was blown far out of proportion by subsequent generations

insights.claim: The Frankish victory at Tours was a temporary setback for the Umayyads, not a decisive halt, since Umayyad forces continued raiding in Gaul and only retreated entirely more than 20 years later.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Directly refutes the claim that Tours stopped Muslim expansion into Europe.
insights.quote: It was a setback for the Umayyads, but a temporary one, and the battle did not ultimately cease Umayyad attacks in Gaul
insights.locator: The army of well-trained, armored Frankish soldiers

insights.claim: Islam's rapid seventh- and eighth-century conquests across Syria, Palestine, North Africa, and Iberia were driven largely by territorial expansion to shore up revenue, with incursions into Gaul in the 720s-730s part of that campaign rather than a religious crusade against Christendom.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Reframes the raids as revenue-driven expansion, undercutting the civilizational-war narrative.
insights.quote: part of that campaign of rapid territorial expansion to shore up revenue

insights.claim: Chronicles from around the time of Tours do not frame it as a religious war, and Tomaz Mastnak argues that for Charlemagne and his contemporaries the Saracens were just one group of enemies among many, not the one that worried them most.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Primary-source evidence shows the civilizational framing was absent at the time and added later.
insights.quote: the Saracens were no more than one group among many, and not the one that worried them the most

insights.claim: The Continuations of the Chronicle of Fredegar records that Odo, duke of Aquitaine, allied with the Muslim Berber governor Munuza and a combined Christian-Muslim force to fight against Charles Martel, showing the real story was internecine Frankish conflict, not Christianity against Islam.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: A concrete Christian-Muslim alliance against Martel dismantles the binary us-versus-them reading of the era.
insights.quote: he summoned to his assistance against Prince Charles and his Franks the unbelieving Saracen people

insights.claim: Wollenberg argues that for Martel, Tours mattered only because it solidified the Franks' hold on their territory and protected their wealth, not as a civilizational duel between East and West.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Locates the battle's real stakes in territory and wealth, the article's core reinterpretation.
insights.quote: It was not a civilizational duel at high noon between East and West or Christianity and Islam.
insights.locator: For Martel, Tours was an important battle

insights.claim: The myth of Tours as a civilizational hinge hardened after Pope Urban II's 1095 call for the First Crusade, when it became commonplace for medieval European texts to frame Islam as evil and to exaggerate the scope of earlier battles in Spain and Gaul.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Dates the myth's origin to Crusade-era propaganda rather than the battle itself.
insights.quote: it became commonplace for medieval European texts to frame the Islamic religion as evil

insights.claim: The circa-1100 Song of Roland turned Charlemagne's 778 incursion into Spain into a civilizational struggle, even though Charlemagne had actually been invited by the Islamic governor of Barcelona to fight the emir of Cordoba.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: A canonical example of literature retrofitting a binary religious war onto a pragmatic alliance.
insights.quote: The pagans are wrong and the Christians are right
insights.locator: Composed around 1100, the fictional chanson de geste

insights.claim: Wollenberg attributes the modern reputation of Tours to 18th- and 19th-century historians, with Edward Gibbon claiming Christendom was delivered by Martel and Sir Edward Creasy claiming Tours re-established the superiority of the Indo-European over the Semitic family of mankind.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Names the specific historiography that seeded the racialized 'saved civilization' narrative.
insights.quote: rescued Christendom from Islam, preserved the relics of ancient and the germs of modern civilization, and re-established the old superiority of the Indo-European over the Semitic family of mankind

themes.theme: Weaponization by the modern far right

insights.claim: Wollenberg argues political discourse on the identitarian far right insists on Tours' monumental significance as the moment Charles Martel saved Christian Europe from Islam, in order to sustain a false narrative of a thousand-year civilizational war.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Identifies the myth's present-day political function, the reason its lifespan endures.
insights.quote: political discourse, especially on the identitarian far right, insists on Tours’ monumental significance on the fate of Christendom and Europe

insights.claim: French New Right founder Guillaume Faye framed Islam as launching three assaults on Europe, halted at Poitiers in 732 and Vienna in 1683 and now underway as a third invasion by immigration seeking to establish a caliphate.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: A concrete example of recasting historical battles as a template for anti-immigration politics.
insights.quote: The first of these offensives was halted at Poitiers in 732 by Charles Martel; the second in 1683, during the Ottoman siege of Vienna; the third … is now underway
insights.locator: Guillaume Faye, a prominent anti-Islam French nationalist

insights.claim: The myth of Tours has been invoked by violent actors, including the Charles Martel Group, a far-right French terrorist organization behind bombings of Algerian consulates in the 1970s and 80s, and the white supremacist who murdered 51 people at two Christchurch mosques in 2019 had 'Tours 732' etched into a rifle.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Documents the direct line from historical myth to real-world terrorist violence, the article's warning.
insights.quote: had “Tours 732” etched into one of his rifles
insights.locator: The white supremacist terrorist who murdered 51 people

insights.claim: Wollenberg argues the deeper danger is not forgetting the past but maliciously 'remembering' it in bad faith to justify contemporary political ends, molding history into an identitarian teleology.
insights.speaker: Daniel Wollenberg
insights.so_what: Generalizes the case into a broader thesis about the political misuse of history.
insights.quote: sometimes it is precisely those who callously and maliciously “remember” the past in bad faith who try to ensure that it is repeated
